name: अक्षरब्रह्मयोग
teaching: What you dwell on, you become — and what fills the mind at the end of life reveals what filled it all along. Krishna speaks plainly about death: the cosmos itself breathes in and out, worlds arise and dissolve, and beyond all of it stands the imperishable, reached by remembrance. Therefore remember now; the final thought is only the sum of every ordinary one. What is held in the mind across a life is what the mind holds at the end — so remembrance is made a daily art. Two paths lead out of the world; the chapter teaches the bright one.
questions: If your last thought will be your most practiced thought, what are you practicing?
What in your life belongs to the cycle that returns, and what to that which does not?
Could you pair one daily act — breath, walking, work — with remembrance, starting today?

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
किं तद् ब्रह्म किमध्यात्मं किं कर्म पुरुषोत्तम ।
अधिभूतं च किं प्रोक्तमधिदैवं किमुच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
kiṃ tad brahma kimadhyātmaṃ kiṃ karma puruṣottama
adhibhūtaṃ ca kiṃ proktamadhidaivaṃ kimucyate
verses.essence: Arjuna asks: what is that Brahman? What is the adhyatma? What is karma, Purushottama? What is called adhibhuta, and what adhidaiva?
verses.translation: What is Brahman? What is Adhyatma? What is action, O best among men? What is Adhibhuta declared to be? And, what is Adhidaiva said to be?

anvaya.parts: अधि (concerning) + आत्मन् (self): 'that which concerns the self'
अधि (concerning) + भूत (beings, elements): 'that which concerns beings'

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter nominative singular (declared)

anvaya.parts: अधि (concerning) + दैव (the divine, gods): 'that which concerns the gods'

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is called)

verses.explanation: Arjuna pounces on the loose threads of 7.29–30 and asks five definitions in two lines — a student's rapid-fire after a teacher's deliberate cliffhanger. The questions look academic; the last one (next verse) will reveal they are anything but.
verses.connection: Sets chapter 8's agenda: Krishna answers these five questions in order in 8.3–4, and 8.2's last question, about death, from 8.5 on.
verses.reflection: Keep Arjuna's habit today: when big words blur — Brahman, karma, adhyatma — stop and ask for definitions.
verses.background: Chapter 8 opens with Arjuna speaking. Krishna ended chapter 7 using terms he did not explain: Brahman, the self, action, and what concerns the elements, the gods and sacrifice. Śrīdhara notes Arjuna now wants to know what each means; this verse carries the first five of his questions.
verses.text_note: The translation of this verse was missing in the source dataset; it is taken from the Sivananda text in the gita/gita dataset.
verses.hook: What does Arjuna ask Krishna to explain about God, the self and action?

views.text: Arjuna is asking about the seven terms the Lord dropped at the close of chapter 7 (7.29–30); the eighth chapter exists to make Brahman, karma and the rest plain.
Arjun asks seven questions about terms Krishna himself introduced at the end of chapter seven: six about the terms and one about remembering God at death.

verses.devanagari:
अधियज्ञः कथं कोऽत्र देहेऽस्मिन्मधुसूदन ।
प्रयाणकाले च कथं ज्ञेयोऽसि नियतात्मभिः॥
verses.transliteration:
adhiyajñaḥ kathaṃ ko'tra dehe'sminmadhusūdana
prayāṇakāle ca kathaṃ jñeyo'si niyatātmabhiḥ
verses.essence: How is the adhiyajna here in this body, Madhusudana? And how, at the time of departure, are you to be known by the self-controlled?
verses.translation: Who and how is Adhiyajna here in this body, O destroyer of Madhu (Krishna)? And how at the time of death, art Thou to be known by the self-controlled?

anvaya.base: अधियज्ञ · that which presides over sacrifice
anvaya.parts: अधि (over, concerning) + यज्ञ (sacrifice): 'the one over sacrifice'

anvaya.base: मधुसूदन · slayer of the demon Madhu
anvaya.parts: मधु (the demon Madhu) + सूदन (slayer): 'slayer of Madhu'

anvaya.form: gerundive (to be known), masculine nominative singular

anvaya.base: नियतात्मन् · one whose mind is controlled
anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, instrumental plural (by)
anvaya.parts: नियत (controlled) + आत्मन् (self, mind): 'those whose minds are controlled'

verses.explanation: The seventh question is the live one: prayāṇa-kāle — at the hour of going. Beneath the terminology, Arjuna is asking what every mortal eventually asks: how does one hold the highest knowledge at the moment everything is being taken away? The whole chapter is the answer to this last question.
verses.connection: Completes the seven questions; the final clause sets the chapter's true subject — dying well.
verses.reflection: Ask the practical question under all theology once today: how is He known at the hour it matters most?
verses.background: Arjuna continues the questions he began in the previous verse. Having asked about Brahman, the self, action, the elements and the gods, he now adds the last two: who governs the sacrifice within the body, and how Krishna is known by the disciplined at the moment of death.
verses.hook: How can God be known at the moment of death, Arjuna asks?

views.text: Sorts the questions by seeker: Brahman, adhyātma and karma concern those seeking release from age and death; adhibhūta and adhidaiva concern seekers of wealth and power; adhiyajña and the dying hour concern all three groups.
Takes adhiyajña as the one in this body who presides over sacrifice, prompts it and gives its fruit; 'sacrifice' stands for all actions, and 'how' asks the manner in which He dwells there.

Reads the last question practically: at death memory fails and the senses grow cold, so how can even a steady mind know the Lord then? The name Madhusudana appeals to the one who removes difficulties.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
अक्षरं ब्रह्म परमं स्वभावोऽध्यात्ममुच्यते ।
भूतभावोद्भवकरो विसर्गः कर्मसंज्ञितः॥
verses.transliteration:
akṣaraṃ brahma paramaṃ svabhāvo'dhyātmamucyate
bhūtabhāvodbhavakaro visargaḥ karmasaṃjñitaḥ
verses.essence: The Imperishable is the supreme Brahman; its presence in each being is the adhyatma; the creative offering that gives rise to beings is called karma.
verses.translation: Brahman is the Imperishable, the Supreme; Its essential nature is called Self-knowledge; the offering (to the gods) which causes existence and manifestation of beings and which also sustains them is called action.

anvaya.base: अक्षर · imperishable, that which does not decay
anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, neuter, nominative singular
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + क्षर (perishing): 'that which does not perish'

anvaya.meaning: the adhyatma, what concerns the self
anvaya.parts: अधि (concerning) + आत्मन् (self): 'that which concerns the self'

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is called)

anvaya.base: भूतभावोद्भवकर · causing the origin of beings
anvaya.parts: भूत (beings) + भाव (existence) + उद्भव (origin) + कर (making): 'that which brings about the origin of beings' existence'

anvaya.form: past participle used as adjective, masculine nominative singular

verses.explanation: Three answers in one breath, each a doorway: Brahman is the akṣara, what cannot be eroded; adhyātma is that same reality as it lives in *you*, your own deepest nature; and karma, in its widest sense, is visarga — the sacrificial pouring-forth by which existence keeps generating existence. Definitions like compressed scriptures.
verses.connection: Its first definition, Brahman as the Imperishable, names the goal the chapter keeps returning to, in 8.11 and again in 8.21.
verses.reflection: Define your terms this morning: the imperishable in you, your inner nature, and the offering you call work.
verses.background: Krishna now begins answering Arjuna's seven questions, in the order Arjuna asked them. Śrīdhara notes the answers run over three verses. This verse takes up the first three: what Brahman is, what is meant by the self, and what action is.
verses.hook: What do Brahman, adhyatma and karma mean, according to Krishna?

refs.note: Sages call Brahman the Imperishable, supreme because it has qualities beyond Maya and souls, matching this verse's definition.

views.text: Akṣara is the supreme immutable Brahman, not the syllable Om; svabhāva is that same Brahman dwelling in every body as the inner Self; visarga is the oblation to the gods, which through rain gives rise to beings.

Akṣara is the essential self freed from Prakṛti, the goal for seekers of kaivalya; adhyātma is one's material nature clinging to the self, to be given up; karma is the procreative act, from which aspirants abstain.
Svabhāva is Consciousness that never ceases in Brahman; 'karma' is that Consciousness's free creative emission, manifesting itself as both insentient and sentient beings.
Svabhāva is Brahman's own portion becoming the jīva, which dwells in the body as enjoyer; visarga is the giving up of substances to a deity, standing for all actions.
Brahman is the Supreme beyond time, space and causation, untouched by change; adhyatma here means one's own self of body, mind and intellect; karma is action that binds the soul to rebirth.

verses.devanagari:
अधिभूतं क्षरो भावः पुरुषश्चाधिदैवतम् ।
अधियज्ञोऽहमेवात्र देहे देहभृतां वर॥
verses.transliteration:
adhibhūtaṃ kṣaro bhāvaḥ puruṣaścādhidaivatam
adhiyajño'hamevātra dehe dehabhṛtāṃ vara
verses.essence: The adhibhuta is perishable existence; the purusha is the adhidaiva; and I myself am the adhiyajna here in the body, best of the embodied.
verses.translation: Adhibhuta (knowledge of the elements) pertains to My perishable Nature and the Purusha or the Soul is the Adhidaiva; I alone am the Adhiyajna here in this body, O best among the embodied (men).

anvaya.base: क्षर · perishing, from √क्षर् · to flow away

anvaya.meaning: the adhidaiva, what concerns the gods
anvaya.parts: अधि (concerning) + दैवत (deity): 'that which concerns the gods'

anvaya.base: अधियज्ञ · that which presides over sacrifice

anvaya.parts: देह (body) + भृत् (bearing): 'those who bear a body'

verses.explanation: The remaining answers, ending in the chapter's quiet thunderclap: adhiyajño 'ham evātra dehe — the lord of sacrifice is *I, here, in this body*. The receiving altar of every offering a person ever makes is not in a temple or a heaven; it is resident within the offerer. All the chapter's death-instruction follows from this nearness.
verses.connection: Completes the definitions and plants the key: the One to be remembered at death already dwells inside.
verses.reflection: See today's world as the perishable basis, and yourself as the witness it plays before.
verses.background: Krishna has defined Brahman, the self and action. He now answers the three remaining definitions Arjuna asked for: what concerns the elements, what concerns the gods, and who governs sacrifice here in the body. Arjuna's final question, about the hour of death, is still ahead.
verses.hook: What are adhibhuta, adhidaiva and adhiyajna, and who dwells in the body?

views.text: Puruṣa here is Hiraṇyagarbha, dwelling in the sun and sustaining the senses of all creatures; adhiyajña is Viṣṇu, the deity of sacrifice, said to be 'in the body' because sacrifice is performed with the body.
Indra and the other gods to whom sacrifices are made form the Lord's body; He dwells in them as their Self, so He alone is the real object of all worship.
Puruṣa is the Self in which all deities are established; the same supreme Self is the enjoyer of every sacrifice and the one dwelling in the body, so two questions are settled at once.
The adhiyajña dwells in this body as the inner controller, prompting acts and giving their fruit, yet unattached and distinct from the jīva, as the two birds on one tree show.
The ever-changing universe is adhibhuta; God as the cosmic person ruling the gods is adhidaiva; as the Supreme Soul in every heart who rewards all acts he is adhiyajna, so all sacrifice is for him.

verses.devanagari:
अन्तकाले च मामेव स्मरन्मुक्त्वा कलेवरम् ।
यः प्रयाति स मद्भावं याति नास्त्यत्र संशयः॥
verses.transliteration:
antakāle ca māmeva smaranmuktvā kalevaram
yaḥ prayāti sa madbhāvaṃ yāti nāstyatra saṃśayaḥ
verses.essence: And whoever, at the end, leaves the body remembering me alone, goes to my being — of this there is no doubt.
verses.translation: And whosoever, leaving the body, goes forth remembering Me alone, at the time of death, he attains My Being: there is no doubt about this.

anvaya.parts: अन्त (end) + काल (time): 'the time of the end'

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine nominative singular (while remembering)

verses.explanation: The central promise, flat and unhedged: whoever leaves the body remembering him alone enters his being — nāsty atra saṁśayaḥ, of this there is no doubt. The last act of attention works as the soul's forwarding address. This one line shaped whole devotional practices: the Name on the lips at the end, the Gita read at the bedside, the daily japa. Yet the next verse adds the realism at once: the final thought is not performed at the end but rehearsed across a lifetime — the deathbed merely publishes the habit. Everything that follows in the chapter, the practice, the syllable, the timing, exists to make that remembrance possible when it matters most.
verses.connection: Answers 8.2's death-question directly; the rest of the chapter is its method and fine print.
verses.reflection: Practice the final thought in advance: end one ordinary day remembering Him, as rehearsal.
verses.background: All six terms are now defined. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as Krishna's answer to Arjuna's last question in 8.2, how he is to be known at the moment of death, giving both the means and its result.
verses.hook: What happens to someone who dies remembering God alone?

views.text: 'Me' is the supreme Lord Viṣṇu and 'my state' is that very Reality; the 'no doubt' answers whether such a one attains Him or not.
In whatever way one meditates on Him, that form one attains, just as the royal sage Bharata became a deer by thinking of a deer at death.
Answers 8.2's last question: remembrance of the inner controller is the means of knowing Him at death, departure by the path of light the passage, and attaining His form the fruit.
One who dies absorbed in God's names, forms, qualities, pastimes and abode attains him and a godlike nature; consciousness at death decides what comes next.

verses.devanagari:
यं यं वापि स्मरन्भावं त्यजत्यन्ते कलेवरम् ।
तं तमेवैति कौन्तेय सदा तद्भावभावितः॥
verses.transliteration:
yaṃ yaṃ vāpi smaranbhāvaṃ tyajatyante kalevaram
taṃ tamevaiti kaunteya sadā tadbhāvabhāvitaḥ
verses.essence: Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, Kaunteya, that very state one attains, ever shaped by that absorption.
verses.translation: Whosoever at the end leaves the body, thinking of any being, to that being only does he go, O son of Kunti (Arjuna), because of his constant thought of that being.

anvaya.form: relative pronoun, masculine accusative singular (doubled for 'whatever')
present participle, masculine nominative singular (while remembering)
pronoun, masculine accusative singular (doubled to match यं यं)

anvaya.base: तद्भावभावित · imbued with the thought of that
anvaya.form: past participle used as adjective, masculine nominative singular
anvaya.parts: तद् (that) + भाव (state, thought) + भावित (imbued, formed): 'one imbued with the thought of that'

verses.explanation: The general law beneath 8.5's special case: whatever state one remembers on leaving the body, to that one goes — the final thought is a vector, and the soul travels along it. But the verse closes its own loophole before anyone games it: sadā tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ, always steeped in that state. The dying thought is not chosen at the deathbed; it is the residue of a lifetime's dwelling, the loudest habit surfacing at the end. One cannot cram for this examination. That is why the doctrine gave rise to the practice of constant remembrance: it abolished last-minute religion.
verses.connection: Generalizes 8.5 into law — and explains why the next verse must say 'at all times'.
verses.reflection: Mind what you marinate in — whatever state you feed daily is the state that will claim the exit.
verses.background: Krishna has promised that whoever dies remembering him reaches him. Śrīdhara introduces this verse as showing that this is not a rule about him alone. Krishna now states the wider principle that governs every death.
verses.hook: What decides where a person goes after leaving the body?

views.text: Tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ means one in whom that entity is a matter of habitual recollection; since the last thought causes the next body, it must be shaped beforehand.
The final thought arises only about objects already ruminated upon in life, which is why the next verse must command remembrance at all times.
Like the caterpillar that becomes the wasp it constantly thinks of, one becomes what one dwells on; Jaḍabharata, thinking of his pet deer, was born a deer.
The thought that dominates the mind at death sets the next birth, and it follows lifelong habit, as King Bharat, absorbed in a fawn, became a deer; so God must be remembered at every moment.

verses.devanagari:
तस्मात्सर्वेषु कालेषु मामनुस्मर युध्य च ।
मय्यर्पितमनोबुद्धिर्मामेवैष्यस्यसंशयः॥
verses.transliteration:
tasmātsarveṣu kāleṣu māmanusmara yudhya ca
mayyarpitamanobuddhirmāmevaiṣyasyasaṃśayaḥ
verses.essence: Therefore at all times remember me, and fight. With mind and understanding surrendered to me, you will come to me — beyond doubt.
verses.translation: Therefore at all times remember Me only and fight. With mind and intellect fixed (or absorbed) in Me, thou shalt doubtlessly come to Me alone.

anvaya.base: अर्पितमनोबुद्धि · one whose mind and intellect are offered
anvaya.parts: अर्पित (offered) + मनस् (mind) + बुद्धि (intellect): 'one whose mind and intellect are given over'

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, nominative singular (used as 'there is no doubt')

verses.explanation: The Gita's whole reconciliation in four words: mām anusmara yudhya ca — remember me, *and fight*. Not remembrance instead of the battle, nor the battle postponing remembrance: both at once, the inner thread unbroken through the outer act. Mayy arpita-mano-buddhiḥ: mind and intellect deposited in him while the hands do their fierce duty. Because the last thought cannot be manufactured at the end (8.6), it must be kept alive 'at all times', and the work of one's own station is where that keeping happens. The verse is the charter of every contemplative-in-action since.
verses.connection: The first of the chapter's two 'at all times' commands; 8.27 repeats it after the two paths, so both teachings end in the same steady practice.
verses.reflection: Carry the full instruction into one task today: remember — and fight. Both, together, all day.
verses.background: Krishna has said that one's final thought, shaped by lifelong habit, decides where one goes. Śrīdhara draws the consequence: a helpless dying person cannot suddenly start remembering. Krishna now turns this to Arjuna himself, standing on the battlefield, and tells him what to do.
verses.text_note: Variant: asaṃśayam (Gita Supersite / Gita Press) for asaṃśayaḥ (critical edition, used here).
verses.hook: How can you remember God and still do your work in the world?

views.text: Thinking of Him while fighting is not a combination of knowledge and action, because when every act, means and result is seen as Brahman, action has no separate reality.
'Fight' means carrying out the duties of one's station day after day, duties that themselves keep one remembering Him until the hour of death.
The Lord, of His own accord, becomes the object of memory at death for one from whose heart He has never departed in any worldly circumstance.
At death one is helpless, so only past impressions bring remembrance; constant remembrance needs a pure mind, and fighting, one's own duty, is what purifies it.
This line holds the Gita's essence: do your duty with the body while the mind stays attached to God. Work done without selfish attachment creates no karmic bondage, as with Arjun's fighting.

verses.devanagari:
अभ्यासयोगयुक्तेन चेतसा नान्यगामिना ।
परमं पुरुषं दिव्यं याति पार्थानुचिन्तयन्॥
verses.transliteration:
abhyāsayogayuktena cetasā nānyagāminā
paramaṃ puruṣaṃ divyaṃ yāti pārthānucintayan
verses.essence: With a mind harnessed by the yoga of practice, straying to nothing else, meditating — one goes to the supreme divine Purusha, Partha.
verses.translation: With the mind not moving towards any other thing, made steadfast by the method of habitual meditation, and constantly meditating, one goes to the Supreme Person, the Resplendent, O Arjuna.

anvaya.meaning: joined to the yoga of practice
anvaya.parts: अभ्यास (practice, repetition) + योग (discipline) + युक्त (joined): 'joined to the discipline of practice'

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine nominative singular (while meditating)

verses.explanation: How 'at all times' becomes feasible: abhyāsa-yoga, the repetition that wears remembrance into a groove until the mind, left alone, flows there by default — nānya-gāminā, not wandering off. Anucintayan: thinking-along, a current of recollection beneath the day's traffic. Constancy is not strain; it is a trained riverbed.
verses.connection: Supplies the training behind 8.7's command: the same practice that 6.35 named as the way to steady a restless mind.
verses.reflection: Give attention one steady channel today; consciousness flows where practice has dug.
verses.background: Kṛṣṇa has just told Arjuna to remember Him at all times and fight, since the last thought decides where one goes at death. Śrīdhara introduces this verse as showing the inner means of that unbroken remembrance: practice, the same thought kept flowing again and again.
verses.hook: How does steady practice of fixing the mind lead to God?

views.text: Abhyāsa is repeating the same kind of thought about Him, uninterrupted by any contrary idea; 'divine' locates the supreme Person in the effulgent region, the solar orb.
Separates the two words: abhyāsa is keeping the mind often in touch with Him throughout the day without neglecting duties, and yoga is the set meditation done daily.
Practice means shutting out thoughts of other kinds and keeping one current of thought on God; the most vital factor is regularity.
Abhyasa means making remembrance of God a constant habit throughout the day's work; what shapes our future is where the mind rests, and a mind fixed on the pure God becomes pure.

verses.devanagari:
कविं पुराणमनुशासितार-
मणोरणीयांसमनुस्मरेद्यः ।
सर्वस्य धातारमचिन्त्यरूप-
मादित्यवर्णं तमसः परस्तात्॥
verses.transliteration:
kaviṃ purāṇamanuśāsitāramaṇoraṇīyāṃsamanusmaredyaḥ
sarvasya dhātāramacintyarūpamādityavarṇaṃ tamasaḥ parastāt
verses.essence: The seer, the ancient, the ruler, subtler than the subtle, supporter of all, of inconceivable form, sun-colored beyond the darkness —
verses.translation: Whosoever meditates on the Omniscient, the Ancient, the Ruler (of the whole world), minuter than an atom, the supporter of all, of inconceivable form, effulgent like the sun and beyond the darkness of ignorance.

anvaya.base: धातृ · supporter, ordainer (√धा · to place, hold)

anvaya.parts: अचिन्त्य (unthinkable) + रूप (form): 'one whose form is beyond thought'
आदित्य (sun) + वर्ण (color): 'one whose color is the sun's'

verses.explanation: What, concretely, to remember: eight facets given as handholds for meditation — the poet-seer who knows all, older than time, ruler of all, smaller than the smallest, holding everything, shaped beyond imagining, and shining āditya-varṇam, sun-colored, on the far side of all darkness. A portrait built to be gazed at, not merely parsed.
verses.connection: Begins the deathbed meditation proper (8.9–13): the object described before the technique.
verses.reflection: Meditate once on the Ancient Seer — subtler than subtle, sun-colored beyond darkness — for one minute.
verses.background: Having said that the practised mind reaches the radiant Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇa now describes that Person, so that Arjuna knows whom to dwell on. This verse opens a two-verse sentence: it gives the qualities of the one remembered, and 8.10 gives the dying moment.
verses.hook: What qualities of God may you meditate on?

views.text: Dhātṛ is the one who dispenses the fruits of action to each creature; 'sun-colored' means He is manifest as eternal Consciousness, like the sun's light, beyond the darkness of ignorance.
'Subtler than the subtle' means subtler than the individual self, and 'sun-colored, beyond darkness' means He has a divine form peculiar to Himself.
The sun-color does not limit the Absolute; the comparison is drawn only because It too transcends the darkness of ignorance, the false notions of form and the like.
'Darkness' is prakṛti, and the Person stands beyond it; His very nature is self-luminous like the sun, lighting itself and everything else.
Meditation may rest on God's names, forms, pastimes or abode; the verse lists eight attributes, from all-seeing and ancient to sun-bright beyond darkness, and the varied paths are united by devotion.

verses.devanagari:
प्रयाणकाले मनसाऽचलेन
भक्त्या युक्तो योगबलेन चैव ।
भ्रुवोर्मध्ये प्राणमावेश्य सम्यक्
स तं परं पुरुषमुपैति दिव्यम्॥
verses.transliteration:
prayāṇakāle manasā'calena bhaktyā yukto yogabalena caiva
bhruvormadhye prāṇamāveśya samyak sa taṃ paraṃ puruṣamupaiti divyam
verses.essence: At the time of departure, with unmoving mind, with devotion and the strength of yoga, fixing the life-breath between the brows — one reaches that supreme divine Purusha.
verses.translation: At the time of death, with unshaken mind, endowed with devotion, by the power of Yoga, fixing the whole life-breath in the middle of the two eyebrows, he reaches that resplendent Supreme Person.

anvaya.form: noun, feminine, genitive dual (of the two)

verses.explanation: The technique at the threshold: mind stilled, heart given, and the life-current gathered upward to the brow-center — the body's own exit ritual. Note the trinity required: bhakti supplies the direction, yoga-bala the strength, acala manas the stillness. Dying is treated here as the final āsana, performable with skill.
verses.connection: Its breath held between the brows is the first form of the dying practice; 8.12–13 give a fuller one, with the breath raised to the head and Om.
verses.reflection: Gather your life-force gently between the brows for a few breaths tonight, with devotion, and rest there.
verses.background: This verse completes the sentence begun in 8.9: after the qualities of the Person to be remembered, Kṛṣṇa turns to the hour of death itself and to what keeps the mind still then. Śrīdhara names that cause as the strength of yoga, which draws the breath to the point between the brows.
verses.hook: At death, how does the yogi of devotion and breath control reach God?

views.text: The mind is first brought under control in the lotus of the heart, then the vital force is raised by the upward nerve and fixed between the brows; bhakti here means deep love.
The steady mind at death is the fruit of a mind purified day after day by yoga joined with bhakti; the meditator then attains His state and a glory like His.
The yogi concentrates on the lower centres, then the heart, then draws the prāṇa up the suṣumnā to the brow; possible only for one who has given his whole life to yoga.

verses.devanagari:
यदक्षरं वेदविदो वदन्ति
विशन्ति यद्यतयो वीतरागाः ।
यदिच्छन्तो ब्रह्मचर्यं चरन्ति
तत्ते पदं संग्रहेण प्रवक्ष्ये॥
verses.transliteration:
yadakṣaraṃ vedavido vadanti viśanti yadyatayo vītarāgāḥ
yadicchanto brahmacaryaṃ caranti tatte padaṃ saṃgraheṇa pravakṣye
verses.essence: That which the Veda-knowers call the Imperishable, which the passion-free ascetics enter, desiring which they live in continence — that state I shall declare to you in brief.
verses.translation: That which is declared Imperishable by those who know the Vedas, that which the self-controlled (ascetics or Sannyasins) and passion-free enter, that desiring which celibacy is practised that goal I will declare to thee in brief.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, neuter, accusative singular
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + क्षर (perishing): 'that which does not perish'

anvaya.base: वेदविद् · one who knows the Veda
anvaya.parts: वेद (Veda) + विद् (knowing): 'those who know the Veda'
वीत (gone) + राग (passion): 'those whose passion is gone'

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine nominative plural (while desiring)

anvaya.base: ब्रह्मचर्य · continence, life of Vedic study
anvaya.parts: ब्रह्मन् (Veda, Brahman) + चर्य (conduct): 'conduct directed to Brahman'

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, instrumental singular (by way of)

verses.explanation: Credentials before the secret: the goal about to be taught is the same one the Upanishadic seers named, the same one renunciates spend lifetimes of austerity approaching. Krishna offers it saṅgraheṇa — in summary — to a man with hours, not decades: the battlefield condensation of the forest's longest curriculum.
verses.connection: Frames 8.12–13 as the distilled essence of the entire ascetic tradition.
verses.reflection: Honor the syllable the renunciates die into — let OM open or close your practice today.
verses.background: Before teaching a practice built on the sacred syllable OM, Kṛṣṇa announces its goal: the Imperishable that the knowers of the Veda speak of and renunciants seek. Śrīdhara presents the verse as a promise, made because He means to teach a discipline closer to the goal than practice alone.
verses.hook: What is the imperishable goal the sages enter, which Krishna will describe briefly?

refs.note: Says the sun and moon stay on course under the command of the Imperishable, the akshara this verse names as the goal.

views.text: Prepares the teaching of Om as name and symbol of Brahman, like an image, given to those of lower and middling understanding; meditation on it leads to liberation in course of time.
Pada is what the mind reaches as its goal; what He will tell briefly is His own nature, explained by all of Vedānta and beyond full description.
Saṅgraha is a means by which the end is grasped, so the Lord promises not just the goal but the means for Arjuna's constant practice.

Krishna speaks only briefly of this path because it is hard and not for everyone: union with the formless Imperishable demands strict celibacy and severe austerity, which conserve energy for practice.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वद्वाराणि संयम्य मनो हृदि निरुध्य च ।
मूर्ध्न्याधायात्मनः प्राणमास्थितो योगधारणाम्॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvadvārāṇi saṃyamya mano hṛdi nirudhya ca
mūrdhnyādhāyātmanaḥ prāṇamāsthito yogadhāraṇām
verses.essence: Closing all the body's gates, confining the mind in the heart, drawing the life-breath into the head, established in yogic concentration —
verses.translation: Having closed all the gates, confined the mind in the heart and fixed the life-breath in the head, engaged in the practice of concentration.

anvaya.base: आ-√स्था · to stand on, resort to

anvaya.parts: योग (yoga) + धारणा (holding, concentration): 'the steady holding of yoga'

verses.explanation: The nine-gated city of 5.13 returns for its final scene: gates closed not in defeat but in ceremony, the mind brought home to the heart, the life-force walked up its inner staircase to the crown. The body, which spent a lifetime opening outward, is folded inward once — deliberately, like a letter being sealed.
verses.connection: The physical liturgy of departure, completing 8.10's brow-center instruction.
verses.reflection: Close the gates briefly today: eyes soft, voice still, heart gathered — the city quieted for its king.
verses.background: Kṛṣṇa now keeps the promise of 8.11 and gives the method with its parts, in a sentence that runs over two verses. This verse carries the first part, the closing down of the body and mind; the syllable and the moment of departure follow in 8.13.
verses.hook: How does a yogi shut out the world to meditate at the end?

views.text: The gates are the doors of perception; the mind is confined in the heart so it cannot spread out, and with it the vital force is raised up the nerve from the heart to the head.
The gates are the sense organs only; 'restraining the mind in the heart' means freedom from attachment, not a physical seat, and the prāṇa in the head is the Self with its power of will.
Closing the gates means taking in no outer objects through the senses, and confining the mind means no longer recalling them; 'head' is taken as the point between the brows.
The world enters the mind through the senses, so meditation requires guarding the body's gates, holding the mind in the heart, and turning it with devotion toward the imperishable Lord.

verses.devanagari:
ओमित्येकाक्षरं ब्रह्म व्याहरन्मामनुस्मरन् ।
यः प्रयाति त्यजन्देहं स याति परमां गतिम्॥
verses.transliteration:
omityekākṣaraṃ brahma vyāharanmāmanusmaran
yaḥ prayāti tyajandehaṃ sa yāti paramāṃ gatim
verses.essence: Uttering Om, the one-syllabled Brahman, and remembering me — whoever departs thus, leaving the body, goes to the supreme goal.
verses.translation: Uttering the one-syllabled Om the Brahman and remembering Me, he who departs, leaving the body, attains to the Supreme Goal.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine nominative singular (while uttering)
present participle, masculine nominative singular (while remembering)
present participle, masculine nominative singular (while leaving)

verses.explanation: The last breath given its word and its thought: Om on the lips — the syllable that is sound's seed and the Veda's whole compressed — and Krishna in the mind. Note the pairing: the impersonal vibration *and* the personal remembrance, together; the Gita declines to choose between them even at the very end.
verses.connection: Ties the yoga of 8.12 back to 8.5's simple rule: even this elaborate departure turns on remembering Krishna as the body is left.
verses.reflection: Sound OM once slowly, remembering what it names — and notice the room it makes.
verses.background: The yogi of 8.12 now sits with senses withdrawn, mind held in the heart and breath raised to the head. This verse completes that sentence with the final act at the moment of leaving the body, and says where such a departure leads.
verses.hook: What does chanting Om while remembering God at death bring?

views.text: 'Leaving the body' qualifies the departure: the soul goes by abandoning the body, not by its own destruction; Om is the name of Brahman, and 'Me' is God whom it signifies.
This path belongs to the seeker of kaivalya: he reaches the pure self freed from Prakṛti, a state akin to the Lord's own, from which there is no return.
Om is Brahman either as the word that names it or as its symbol, like an image; uttering it while remembering what it names, one goes by the path of light to the highest goal.

Om, the primal sound of creation, stands for God's formless aspect and is the object of meditation in ashtanga yoga; devotees find more sweetness in God's personal names, and Krishna next offers an easier path.

verses.devanagari:
अनन्यचेताः सततं यो मां स्मरति नित्यशः ।
तस्याहं सुलभः पार्थ नित्ययुक्तस्य योगिनः॥
verses.transliteration:
ananyacetāḥ satataṃ yo māṃ smarati nityaśaḥ
tasyāhaṃ sulabhaḥ pārtha nityayuktasya yoginaḥ
verses.essence: For the one who remembers me constantly with undivided mind — for that ever-harnessed yogi, Partha, I am easy to reach.
verses.translation: I am easily attainable by that ever-steadfast Yogi who constantly and daily remembers Me (for a long time), not thinking of anything else (with a single mind or one-pointed mind), O Partha (Arjuna).

anvaya.base: अनन्यचेतस् · one whose mind goes to no other
anvaya.parts: अनन्य (no other) + चेतस् (mind): 'one whose mind turns to nothing else'

verses.explanation: After the technical rigor of 8.10–13, a verse of pure relief: sulabhaḥ — *easy* to reach. The elaborate death-technique is the hard road for those who need it; for the one whose remembrance never stopped, no technique is required, because nothing was ever put down that must now be picked up. Love makes the examination open-book.
verses.connection: Returns to 8.7's 'at all times': for the one who remembers Krishna daily, with no other thought, reaching Krishna is easy.
verses.reflection: Test the promise of nearness today: hold Him in mind, undivided, for one unbroken hour — a small start on a lifelong constancy.
verses.background: After the demanding procedure of the dying yogi in 8.12–13, Kṛṣṇa turns to the one for whom He is easy to reach. Śrīdhara introduces it as a reminder of what was said before: reaching Him at death by such concentration comes only through daily, lifelong practice.
verses.hook: Who finds God easy to reach?

refs.note: Krishna says to take refuge in him alone, the soul of all beings, supporting exclusive devotion as the way to reach him.
A devotee says Ram is his only support, strength, hope and faith, an example of the undivided mind the verse asks for.
Defines exclusiveness as giving up all other shelters, the condition for God being easy to attain.

views.text: Satatam means without any break and nityaśaḥ means for a long time: not six months or a year, but one's whole life.
Such a devotee cannot sustain himself without remembering Him; the Lord Himself removes obstacles and grants the maturity of devotion, since 'whom He chooses, by him He is obtained'.
Doubts the need for any upward flight of the soul: if Śiva is everywhere, the upward flight serves no purpose, and constant remembrance itself is the realisation of His state.
Recalls the earlier point: the concentration at death that wins Him comes only through daily practice, and He is easily reached by that one and no other.

For the first time Krishna calls himself easy to attain, but only for those whose mind is exclusively on him; love for God mixed with worldly attachment is like washing a cloth and dipping it back in dirt.

verses.devanagari:
मामुपेत्य पुनर्जन्म दुःखालयमशाश्वतम् ।
नाप्नुवन्ति महात्मानः संसिद्धिं परमां गताः॥
verses.transliteration:
māmupetya punarjanma duḥkhālayamaśāśvatam
nāpnuvanti mahātmānaḥ saṃsiddhiṃ paramāṃ gatāḥ
verses.essence: Having come to me, the great souls do not take rebirth in this impermanent house of sorrow — they have reached the highest perfection.
verses.translation: Having attained Me these great souls do not again take birth (here) which is the place of pain and is non-eternal: they have reached the highest perfection (liberation).

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine nominative plural (having gone)

verses.explanation: The destination's permanence, with the world given its bleakest honest epithets in passing: duḥkhālayam aśāśvatam — a lodging of sorrow, and a temporary one at that. Not a curse upon existence but a traveler's accurate review of the inn. Those who reach him do not check back in.
verses.connection: Its promise of no rebirth is the line 8.16 extends to every world and 8.21 attaches to Krishna's own highest abode.
verses.reflection: Hold the destination clearly: reached once, the house of sorrow is not re-entered.
verses.background: Kṛṣṇa has just said He is easy to reach for one who remembers Him without break. Śaṅkara frames this verse as the answer to Arjuna's natural next question: what follows from Your being easy to reach? Here He states what becomes of those who arrive.
verses.hook: What happens to those who reach God?

views.text: The great souls are the monks who have realised His nature; the perfection is liberation, and the birth they escape is both a resort of sorrows and without fixity.
These great souls know His nature truly and cannot sustain themselves without Him, so they take Him alone as the goal and are freed from rebirth.
Reads 'having attained Me' as gradual liberation: devotees go by the path of the gods to Brahma's world and are freed with Brahma at the cosmic dissolution.
Life from womb to death is full of suffering, which works like the pain of a burn: a signal to turn from the world. Souls who reach God through exclusive devotion never return to it.

verses.devanagari:
आब्रह्मभुवनाल्लोकाः पुनरावर्तिनोऽर्जुन ।
मामुपेत्य तु कौन्तेय पुनर्जन्म न विद्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
ābrahmabhuvanāllokāḥ punarāvartino'rjuna
māmupetya tu kaunteya punarjanma na vidyate
verses.essence: All worlds up to the realm of Brahma are subject to return, Arjuna. But having come to me, Kaunteya, there is no rebirth.
verses.translation: (All) the worlds including the world of Brahma are subject to return again, O Arjuna; but he who reaches Me, O son of Kunti, has no rebirth.

anvaya.base: आब्रह्मभुवन · as far as Brahma's realm
anvaya.form: noun, neuter, ablative singular (with आ: up to)
anvaya.parts: आ (up to) + ब्रह्मन् (Brahmā, the creator) + भुवन (world): 'up to and including the world of Brahmā'

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is found)

verses.explanation: The cosmic ceiling drawn: even Brahma's own realm — the summit of every ladder austerity can climb — is on the circuit; its residents, however exalted, hold return tickets. One destination alone is exempt. The verse quietly devalues every heaven in advance: anything reachable by merit is rentable, not ownable.
verses.connection: Extends 8.15 upward through the entire cosmos: all stations revolve except the hub.
verses.reflection: Stop renovating rooms in burning buildings — even the highest worlds return; aim past them today.
verses.background: Having said that those who reach Him are not born again, Kṛṣṇa takes up the implied question Śaṅkara puts: do those who reach anything else come back? He answers for every world, even the realm of Brahmā, the creator, which seems the highest goal of all.
verses.hook: Is any world, even the highest heaven, free from rebirth?

views.text: All worlds, Brahma's included, come back because they are limited by time, which the next verse goes on to measure.
Rejects the usual reading: ā-brahma means 'until the supreme Brahman is attained'; till then beings circle like a wheel from every world, high or low.

Brahma's world also perishes, so those who reach it without knowledge are reborn; only those who reach it through meditations meant for gradual liberation, and gain knowledge there, are freed along with Brahma.
All fourteen worlds, up to Brahma's, lie within Maya, so even Indra must die, as the stories of the ant-Indras and Rishi Lomash show; only reaching God ends rebirth.

verses.devanagari:
सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद् ब्रह्मणो विदुः ।
रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः॥
verses.transliteration:
sahasrayugaparyantamaharyad brahmaṇo viduḥ
rātriṃ yugasahasrāntāṃ te'horātravido janāḥ
verses.essence: Those who know Brahma's day to last a thousand ages, and his night a thousand ages — they are the knowers of day and night.
verses.translation: Those people who know the day of Brahma which is of a duration of a thousand Yugas (ages) and the night which is also of a thousand Yugas duration, they know day and night.

anvaya.base: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्त · ending with a thousand yugas
anvaya.parts: सहस्र (thousand) + युग (age) + पर्यन्त (limit): 'having a thousand ages as its limit'

anvaya.form: verb, perfect with present sense, 3rd person plural

anvaya.base: युगसहस्रान्त · ending in a thousand yugas
anvaya.parts: युग (age) + सहस्र (thousand) + अन्त (end): 'whose end comes after a thousand ages'

anvaya.base: अहोरात्रविद् · one who knows day and night
anvaya.parts: अहन् (day) + रात्र (night) + विद् (knowing): 'those who know day and night'

verses.explanation: The scale of 8.16's wheel: one working day of the creator spans a thousand cosmic ages, his night the same — our worlds bloom at his dawn and are folded away at his dusk. Whoever has internalized *this* calendar, the verse says drily, actually knows what 'day and night' mean; everyone else is reading a child's clock.
verses.connection: Begins the cosmological zoom-out (8.17–19) that makes 8.16's 'return' visible at full scale.
verses.reflection: Zoom out once today: your busiest year is a flicker in Brahma's single day. Breathe accordingly.
verses.background: Why should even Brahmā's realm send its dwellers back? Śaṅkara's answer is that every world is bounded by time. To show how, Kṛṣṇa first gives the measure of the creator's day and night, spans of time beyond human reckoning.
verses.hook: How long are Brahma's day and night?

views.text: The knowers of day and night are those who know the measure of time; since the worlds are bounded by such time, they are subject to return.
The three worlds arise every day of Brahma and dissolve every night; the true knowers of day and night know this through yoga, not merely from the course of sun and moon.
Sets out the reckoning: a mahāyuga of 4,320,000 years, a thousand of them a day of Brahma, an equal night, and a lifetime of a hundred such years; even Brahma's world is transient.
Vedic time is vast: a day of Brahma is a thousand cycles of four ages, about 4.32 billion years, with a night as long. Even Brahma is a soul subject to birth and death.

verses.devanagari:
अव्यक्ताद् व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे ।
रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके॥
verses.transliteration:
avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavantyaharāgame
rātryāgame pralīyante tatraivāvyaktasaṃjñake
verses.essence: At the coming of day, all manifest things stream forth from the unmanifest; at the coming of night they dissolve into that same unmanifest.
verses.translation: From the Unmanifested all the manifested (worlds) proceed at the coming of the 'day'; at the coming of the 'night' they dissolve verily into that alone which is called the Unmanifested.

anvaya.meaning: in what is called the unmanifest
anvaya.parts: अव्यक्त (unmanifest) + संज्ञक (named): 'that which is named the unmanifest'

verses.explanation: The cosmic respiration: dawn of Brahma's day and the worlds exhale into form; his dusk, and they are inhaled back into the formless reservoir. Creation and dissolution lose their drama at this magnification — they are breathing, regular as tide, neither a beginning to celebrate nor an end to mourn.
verses.connection: The rhythm inside 8.17's calendar: manifestation as the universe's inhale and exhale.
verses.reflection: Watch one thing emerge this morning and dissolve this evening — the cosmic tide in miniature.
verses.background: The length of Brahmā's day and night has just been given. Śaṅkara introduces this verse as telling what happens during that day and that night: Kṛṣṇa describes the world appearing and disappearing, the "unmanifest" here being its dormant, seed-like state.
verses.hook: What happens to the manifest world at the start and end of Brahma's day?

refs.note: Shukdev compares Brahma creating and dissolving the worlds to a child building toys by day and pulling them apart at night.

views.text: The unmanifest here is the sleep-state of Prajāpati: when Brahma wakes, all moving and unmoving things appear; when he sleeps, they merge back into it.
What appears and dissolves are the beings of the three worlds with their bodies, senses and objects, and the unmanifest is the condition of Brahma's body at that time.
The unmanifest is the causal form of the effect; manifest beings are so called because they are made manifest from that cause and return into it.

Worlds below a certain level dissolve at the end of each day of Brahma and are recreated at dawn; at the end of his life all matter returns to Maha Vishnu, from whose breath infinite universes come and go.

verses.devanagari:
भूतग्रामः स एवायं भूत्वा भूत्वा प्रलीयते ।
रात्र्यागमेऽवशः पार्थ प्रभवत्यहरागमे॥
verses.transliteration:
bhūtagrāmaḥ sa evāyaṃ bhūtvā bhūtvā pralīyate
rātryāgame'vaśaḥ pārtha prabhavatyaharāgame
verses.essence: This very same multitude of beings, arising again and again, dissolves helplessly at the coming of night, Partha, and streams forth at the coming of day.
verses.translation: This same multitude of beings, being born again and again, is dissolved, helplessly, O Arjuna (into the Unmanifested) at the coming of the night and comes forth at the coming of the day.

anvaya.parts: भूत (being) + ग्राम (multitude): the multitude made of beings
रात्रि (night) + आगम (arrival): the arrival of night

anvaya.base: अवश · not in one's own control
anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, nominative singular (describes the multitude)

anvaya.parts: अहन् (day) + आगम (arrival): the arrival of day

verses.explanation: The verse's quiet horror is one word: avaśaḥ — *helplessly*. The same crowd of beings, bhūtvā bhūtvā, becoming and becoming, swept out and swept back with no vote in either direction. This is samsara seen from orbit: not a personal journey but a tide, and everyone unliberated is foam on it. The exit of 8.15 suddenly looks less like doctrine and more like rescue.
verses.connection: Personalizes 8.18's rhythm: the breathing cosmos, seen from inside, is compulsory recurrence.
verses.reflection: Notice one recurrence that runs you helplessly, rising and setting on its own, and let seeing it breed dispassion, not comfort.
verses.background: Kṛṣṇa presses the cycle home. Śrīdhara says the verse shows the stream of creation and dissolution as unbroken, to foster detachment and to answer a doubt: that deeds might vanish unrewarded, or that beings might suffer what they never earned. The beings who return are the very ones who left.

views.text: The very same multitude of beings, moving and non-moving, from the earlier cycle, not any other, dissolves at nightfall and comes to life again at daybreak, without any independence at all.
The multitude is driven by karma; for every entity except the Lord, origination and dissolution are unavoidable, even Brahmā's world. Only those who attain Him are free of return.
No new souls are released at each dawn: the same selves wake to their activities and, at night, rest solely as the Energy of the Absolute.

The verse shows the unbroken stream of creation and dissolution to rouse dispassion, and to rule out that deeds go unreaped or that one reaps what one never did: the same beings return, bound by karma.
Scripture counts four dissolutions: deep sleep, the end of Brahma's day, the end of his life, and final release from Maya when the soul attains God; only the last ends the cycle.

verses.hook: Do beings have any choice as they appear and vanish with each cosmic cycle?

verses.devanagari:
परस्तस्मात्तु भावोऽन्योऽव्यक्तोऽव्यक्तात्सनातनः ।
यः स सर्वेषु भूतेषु नश्यत्सु न विनश्यति॥
verses.transliteration:
parastasmāttu bhāvo'nyo'vyakto'vyaktātsanātanaḥ
yaḥ sa sarveṣu bhūteṣu naśyatsu na vinaśyati
verses.essence: But beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal unmanifest existence — which does not perish when all beings perish.
verses.translation: But verily there exists, higher than this Unmanifested, another unmanifested Eternal, which is not destroyed when all beings are destroyed.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, locative plural (when ..., with the participle)
present participle, neuter, locative plural (while they perish)

verses.explanation: Past the reservoir into which worlds dissolve stands a second unmanifest — avyakto 'vyaktāt — not the seed-state of things but what never entered the cycle at all. The first unmanifest is night between days; this one is what neither day nor night touch. When even the dissolution dissolves, this remains, undented.
verses.connection: Reuses 8.18's word 'Unmanifested' for something higher: not the dormant state the worlds sink into each night, but one that does not perish with them.
verses.reflection: Lean once today on what does not perish when all manifestation perishes — it is nearer than the news.
verses.background: With the impermanence of every world laid out, Kṛṣṇa turns from what perishes to what does not. Śrīdhara says that, having expanded on the transience of the worlds, He now expands on the eternity of the Lord's own nature, over this verse and the next.

views.text: The first unmanifest is ignorance (avidyā), the seed of all beings; this other bhāva is the supreme Brahman, the Immutable, different in kind and not destroyed when everything from Brahmā down perishes.
Takes this second unmanifest as the individual self in its pure form of knowledge, beyond inert prakṛti; it is called unmanifest because no ordinary means of knowledge grasps it.
This is the Lord's own nature: the cause even of the unmanifest that causes the moving and unmoving, beyond the reach of the eye and senses, and without beginning.
Beyond the perishing material worlds lies an eternal spiritual realm made by Yogmaya, which never dissolves, and which Krishna later says forms three-fourths of his creation.

verses.hook: Is there anything that survives when the whole universe dissolves?

verses.devanagari:
अव्यक्तोऽक्षर इत्युक्तस्तमाहुः परमां गतिम् ।
यं प्राप्य न निवर्तन्ते तद्धाम परमं मम॥
verses.transliteration:
avyakto'kṣara ityuktastamāhuḥ paramāṃ gatim
yaṃ prāpya na nivartante taddhāma paramaṃ mama
verses.essence: That unmanifest, called the Imperishable, they declare the supreme goal — attaining which, none return. That is my highest abode.
verses.translation: What is called the Unmanifested and the Imperishable, That they say is the highest goal. They who reach It do not return (to this Samsara). That is My highest abode (place or state).

anvaya.base: thus; marks a quotation or name

anvaya.form: past passive participle, masculine, nominative singular (said, called)
verb, perfect with present sense, 3rd person plural

verses.explanation: The chapter's threads tie: the akṣara of Krishna's first answer (8.3), the unfalling state of 8.20, and now a personal possessive that changes everything — dhāma paramaṁ *mama*. The Beyond-the-beyond is not a vacancy; it is his home address. The Absolute has a host.
verses.connection: Its 'do not return' is the promise 8.15–16 made for reaching Krishna, so the Imperishable goal and his own abode turn out to be one.
verses.reflection: Note where your roads lead: most loop back; one does not. Take three steps on the no-return road today.
verses.background: Kṛṣṇa ties the eternal unmanifest of 8.20 to the Imperishable He promised to describe in 8.11. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as giving the evidence that it never perishes: scripture calls it the supreme goal, from which there is no return, and Kṛṣṇa claims it as His own.

views.text: The unmanifest called the Immutable is the supreme goal, and 'my supreme abode' means the supreme state of Viṣṇu; reaching that Reality, none return to worldly life.
The abode is the freed self in its own nature, the highest object of the Lord's rule; or dhāma means luminosity, the boundless knowledge of the liberated self.
The genitive in 'my abode' is figurative, like 'Rāhu's head': the abode is the Lord's own nature, so He Himself is the supreme goal.
He describes a divine spiritual sky holding the eternal abodes of God's many forms; a devotee who realizes any of these forms reaches its abode, receives a divine body and never returns.

verses.hook: What is the highest goal, the place from which no one returns?

verses.devanagari:
पुरुषः स परः पार्थ भक्त्या लभ्यस्त्वनन्यया ।
यस्यान्तःस्थानि भूतानि येन सर्वमिदं ततम्॥
verses.transliteration:
puruṣaḥ sa paraḥ pārtha bhaktyā labhyastvananyayā
yasyāntaḥsthāni bhūtāni yena sarvamidaṃ tatam
verses.essence: That supreme Purusha, Partha, within whom all beings dwell and by whom all this is pervaded, is attainable by undivided devotion.
verses.translation: That highest Purusha, O Arjuna, is attainable by unswerving devotion to Him alone within Whom all beings dwell and by Whom all this is pervaded.

anvaya.form: noun, feminine, instrumental singular (by means of)
gerundive, masculine, nominative singular (to be attained)
relative pronoun, masculine, genitive singular (of whom)
past passive participle, neuter, nominative singular (pervaded)

verses.explanation: How the unreachable is reached: bhaktyā tv ananyayā — by love with no second object. Not by the cosmological knowledge just displayed, not by austerity that scales only to Brahma's revolving realm: devotion alone crosses into the abode. The chapter that began with seven philosophical definitions answers, in the end, with one relationship.
verses.connection: Gives 8.21's abode its single key — anticipating 11.54's identical claim at the vision's end.
verses.reflection: Try the stated price of the Supreme today: devotion without a second object — bhaktya labhyas tv ananyaya.
verses.background: Kṛṣṇa has named His supreme abode, the place of no return. The next step is how it is gained. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as restating what was said in 8.14: that devotion is the inner means of reaching it.

views.text: The one-pointed devotion is knowledge directed to the Self. Beings rest in the Person as effects in their cause, and He pervades all as space pervades pots.
The Absolute is beyond time yet immanent in all beings; it is called unmanifest because it is hard to attain, and devotion is the means already named.
Ananyā means devotion with no other refuge: the Lord is reached by single-minded bhakti alone, not otherwise, and He is the cause within which all beings stand.
An all-pervading God is hard to love, so worshipping His personal form purifies the heart and draws His grace; only exclusive devotion, by no other path, lets one know Him.

verses.hook: How can the Supreme, who pervades everything, actually be reached?

refs.note: God says He is attained only by devotees who worship Him with faith and love, matching this verse's claim that He is reached through single-minded devotion.
Yoga, austerity, knowledge and detachment cannot reach God without loving devotion, supporting the verse's stress on devotion alone.
Action, knowledge and yoga all depend on devotion to bear fruit, so devotion is the one indispensable path the verse names.

verses.devanagari:
यत्र काले त्वनावृत्तिमावृत्तिं चैव योगिनः ।
प्रयाता यान्ति तं कालं वक्ष्यामि भरतर्षभ॥
verses.transliteration:
yatra kāle tvanāvṛttimāvṛttiṃ caiva yoginaḥ
prayātā yānti taṃ kālaṃ vakṣyāmi bharatarṣabha
verses.essence: Now I shall tell you, Bharatarshabha, the times at which yogis departing return — and do not return.
verses.translation: Now I will tell thee, O chief of Bharatas, the times departing at which the Yogis will return or not return.

anvaya.parts: भरत (Bharata's line) + ऋषभ (bull, best): best of the Bharatas

verses.explanation: A final technical appendix is announced: the traditional lore of departure-times, the cosmic schedule by which the dying are said to be routed. Krishna includes the old map — Arjuna's world knew and trusted it — before quietly relativizing it at the section's end.
verses.connection: Promises the two departures that 8.24 and 8.25 describe and 8.26 sums up; 8.27 then turns them into counsel for Arjuna.
verses.reflection: Live one day so the hour of departure could fall anywhere in it without finding you unready.
verses.background: It has been said that the Lord's worshippers reach Him and do not return, while others return. Śrīdhara sets up the obvious question: by which path do the departed not return, and by which do they come back? Kṛṣṇa promises to tell Arjuna both "times" of departure.

views.text: 'Yogis' covers both meditators and men of ritual action; the latter are called yogis only by courtesy, as in 'the yoga of action for the yogis' (3.3).
'Time' here stands for a path, marked by deities who preside over divisions of time from day to year; one path is for yogis who do not return, the other for doers of good works who do.
He reads the two paths as an allegory: light stands for knowledge and detachment that lead to God, darkness for worldly attachment that keeps the soul returning to birth and death.

verses.hook: At what times do yogis who die return, and when do they not?

verses.devanagari:
अग्निर्ज्योतिरहः शुक्लः षण्मासा उत्तरायणम् ।
तत्र प्रयाता गच्छन्ति ब्रह्म ब्रह्मविदो जनाः॥
verses.transliteration:
agnirjyotirahaḥ śuklaḥ ṣaṇmāsā uttarāyaṇam
tatra prayātā gacchanti brahma brahmavido janāḥ
verses.essence: Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the sun's northern course — departing then, the knowers of Brahman go to Brahman.
verses.translation: Fire, light daytime, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern path of the sun (the northern solstice) departing then (by these) men who know Brahman go to Brahman.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular (pakṣa, fortnight, understood)

anvaya.base: उत्तरायण · northward course of the sun

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, nominative plural (describes the people)
anvaya.parts: ब्रह्म (Brahman) + विद् (knower): those who know Brahman

verses.explanation: The luminous itinerary: every station on this route is a form of light — flame, brightness, day, waxing moon, the sun climbing north. Read literally, a calendar; the classical commentators read each station as a presiding deity on the Upanishads' path of the gods, guiding the soul upward stage by stage. Either way the route is made of light — of knowledge — and those who leave by it do not come back.
verses.connection: Its stages of light, fire, day, bright fortnight and northern sun, are mirrored stage by stage in 8.25's path of return.
verses.reflection: Walk the bright path in miniature today: act in daylight clarity, openly, with nothing to hide.
verses.background: Having promised to describe both ways of departing, Kṛṣṇa gives first the path of no return, in the old language of the Upanishads, which map the soul's journey at death in stages. Śrīdhara reads each named stage as the deity who presides over it.

views.text: Each station is a deity presiding over time, and the 'knowers' are meditators on qualified Brahman who reach it by stages. The fully realized have no going at all: they are Brahman here.
The upward course is described figuratively by words like fire and day because of its illuminating nature; the opposite course gets the opposite terms.

The names point to the Upanishadic deities of flame, day, waxing fortnight and northern half-year, and stand in for the rest of the route given in śruti (year, world of the gods); devotees of the Lord travel it to Brahman.
The path of light symbolizes knowledge and discrimination; God-conscious souls who leave the world detached travel it, are freed from rebirth and reach God's divine abode.

verses.hook: Which path at death leads the knowers of the Absolute to it?

verses.devanagari:
धूमो रात्रिस्तथा कृष्णः षण्मासा दक्षिणायनम् ।
तत्र चान्द्रमसं ज्योतिर्योगी प्राप्य निवर्तते॥
verses.transliteration:
dhūmo rātristathā kṛṣṇaḥ ṣaṇmāsā dakṣiṇāyanam
tatra cāndramasaṃ jyotiryogī prāpya nivartate
verses.essence: Smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the six months of the southern course — departing then, the yogi attains the lunar light and returns.
verses.translation: Attaining to the lunar light by smoke, night time, the dark fortnight also, the six months of the southern path of the sun (the southern solstice), the Yogi returns.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular (pakṣa, fortnight, understood)

anvaya.base: दक्षिणायन · southward course of the sun

verses.explanation: The mirrored route, every station dimmed: smoke for fire, night for day, waning for waxing, the sun's southern retreat. Its terminus is the moon's borrowed light — merit's heaven, lovely and finite — from which the traveler nivartate, comes back. Departure through dimness, through works without knowledge, circles home again.
verses.connection: The path of return: the same journey taken through shadow instead of light.
verses.reflection: Notice your smoke-path hours — the dim, half-asleep ones — and reclaim one of them for clarity.
verses.background: Now Kṛṣṇa gives the second path, the one that leads back. Śrīdhara says it is taken by the doer of rites, who reaches heaven, enjoys the fruit of his sacrifices and good works there, and then returns to birth.

views.text: The 'yogi' here is the man of sacrifices and rites; reaching the lunar light, he enjoys the fruit of his works and returns when it is exhausted.
Desire-driven works lead by this path to heaven and back; forbidden deeds lead to hell and back; only meditation joined to selfless works leads to gradual liberation.
Smoke, night and the dark fortnight may also stand for degrees of ignorance, attachment and passion: a route with no illumination, reached through ignorance.
The dark path stands for ignorance and bodily identification; souls attached to the world, even ritualists who reach the heavens, must return to earth once their merit runs out.

verses.hook: Which path at death brings a person back to this world again?

verses.devanagari:
शुक्लकृष्णे गती ह्येते जगतः शाश्वते मते ।
एकया यात्यनावृत्तिमन्ययावर्तते पुनः॥
verses.transliteration:
śuklakṛṣṇe gatī hyete jagataḥ śāśvate mate
ekayā yātyanāvṛttimanyayāvartate punaḥ
verses.essence: These two paths of the world — the bright and the dark — are held to be eternal. By one, a person goes never to return; by the other, returns again.
verses.translation: The bright and the dark paths of the world are verily thought to be eternal; by the one (the bright path) a man goes not to return and by the other (the dark path) he returns.

anvaya.parts: शुक्ल (bright) + कृष्ण (dark): the bright one and the dark one

anvaya.form: past passive participle, feminine, nominative dual (considered)

verses.explanation: The two itineraries stamped as permanent fixtures of the cosmos: śukla and kṛṣṇa, the bright way and the dark, always open, always carrying their respective traffic. Beneath the old astronomy, a clean fork: knowledge exits, merit revolves. Whoever walks either road, the seeker of knowledge or the doer of rites, is on a route whose end is already fixed.
verses.connection: Reduces 8.24–25 to one split, going without return or returning, the same split 8.15–16 drew between reaching Krishna and reaching any other world.
verses.reflection: Both paths are eternal but not equal; choose, in one decision today, the one of light.
verses.background: Both paths have now been described, the bright one of 8.24 and the dark one of 8.25. Śrīdhara introduces this verse as Kṛṣṇa's summing up of the two before He draws a lesson from them for Arjuna.

views.text: The path is white because it reveals knowledge, black because that revelation is absent; both are eternal because worldly existence is, yet they open only to those qualified for knowledge or for rites.
Śruti names who takes each: those who worship with faith and austerity in the forest go to the light; those in the village who do meritorious works and give alms pass to the smoke (Chāndogya 5.10).
Every soul at death takes one of the two paths, light or darkness, and its own karma decides which; one leads to liberation, the other back into the cycle of birth.

verses.hook: Are the bright and dark paths permanent features of the world?

verses.devanagari:
नैते सृती पार्थ जानन्योगी मुह्यति कश्चन ।
तस्मात्सर्वेषु कालेषु योगयुक्तो भवार्जुन॥
verses.transliteration:
naite sṛtī pārtha jānanyogī muhyati kaścana
tasmātsarveṣu kāleṣu yogayukto bhavārjuna
verses.essence: Knowing these two paths, Partha, no yogi is deluded. Therefore at all times, Arjuna, be steadfast in yoga.
verses.translation: Knowing these paths, O Arjuna, no Yogi is deluded; therefore at all times be steadfast in Yoga.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while knowing)
pronoun, ablative singular used as indeclinable (therefore)

anvaya.parts: योग (yoga) + युक्त (joined): one joined in yoga

verses.explanation: The lore's practical cash-value, and it is deliberately deflating: knowing the schedule frees one from anxiety about the schedule. The yogi does not time his death to the bright fortnight; he makes himself bright at all times — sarveṣu kāleṣu, the chapter's refrain returning — so that any hour of departure is the right one.
verses.connection: Resolves the two-paths teaching the same way 8.7 resolved the final-thought law: constancy beats timing.
verses.reflection: Let knowledge of the two paths remove anxiety, not add it — the yogi knows, and is not bewildered.
verses.background: Kṛṣṇa turns the two paths into counsel for Arjuna, who still stands on the battlefield. Śrīdhara says He states the fruit of knowing the paths and so concludes the teaching on devotion: the one who knows them no longer hankers after heaven.

views.text: Knowing the two courses, one leading to worldly life and the other to Liberation, no yogi is deluded; so Arjuna should be steadfast in Yoga at all times.
The undeluded yogi goes by the path of the gods as his own; so Arjuna is told to meditate every day on that path of light.
The yogi knows the two courses by an internal method of yoga: the 'times' are inner units of time, and one practises yoga connected with them all.
Not being deluded means not craving heaven and its pleasures as if they were happiness; knowing the two paths, the yogi stays fixed on the Lord alone.
Keeping to the path of light for a while is not enough, since one easily drifts back into darkness; that is why Krishna says to be a yogi at all times, continuously.

verses.hook: What does knowing the two paths do for a yogi?

verses.devanagari:
वेदेषु यज्ञेषु तपःसु चैव
दानेषु यत्पुण्यफलं प्रदिष्टम् ।
अत्येति तत्सर्वमिदं विदित्वा
योगी परं स्थानमुपैति चाद्यम्॥
verses.transliteration:
vedeṣu yajñeṣu tapaḥsu caiva dāneṣu yatpuṇyaphalaṃ pradiṣṭam
atyeti tatsarvamidaṃ viditvā yogī paraṃ sthānamupaiti cādyam
verses.essence: Whatever fruit of merit is assigned to the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and gifts — the yogi who knows this passes beyond it all, and reaches the supreme primal abode.
verses.translation: Whatever fruit of merit is declared (in the scriptures) to accrue from (the study of) the Vedas, (the performance of) sacrifices, (the practice of) austerities, and gifts beyond all this goes the Yogi, having known this; and he attains to the Supreme Primeval (first or ancient) Abode.

noun, masculine, locative plural (in regard to)
noun, neuter, locative plural (in regard to)
noun, neuter, locative plural (in regard to)

anvaya.parts: पुण्य (merit) + फल (fruit): the fruit of merit

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, nominative singular (declared)
pronoun, neuter, accusative singular (object of knowing)

verses.explanation: The chapter's closing audit: tally every reward scripture ever promised — Vedic recitation, sacrifice, austerity, charity — and the knower of this teaching atyeti, overtakes the whole column. Not by despising those goods but by aiming past their ceiling: they purchase the revolving heavens of 8.16; this knowledge purchases the ādya sthāna, the first and final home.
verses.connection: Sets the merit of Vedas, rites, austerities and gifts against 8.21's abode, the one goal from which, unlike the worlds of 8.16, none return.
verses.reflection: Aim past all listed merits today — study, rites, gifts, austerity — to what makes them small.
verses.background: This is the last verse of chapter 8, which answered the questions Arjuna asked at its start, ending with how the Lord is known at the hour of death. Śrīdhara introduces it as the chapter's conclusion, stating the fruit of knowing those answers.

views.text: Having fully understood and practised what was taught in answering Arjuna's seven questions, the yogi goes beyond all the merit of Vedic study, sacrifice, austerity and charity, and reaches the primordial State of God, Brahman.
'This' is the Lord's greatness taught in chapters 7 and 8; the joy of knowing it makes the yogi regard every promised reward as worthless as straw.
He 'goes beyond' by constant remembrance of the Lord, which neutralizes the impressions left by all actions; with them gone, he easily attains the Supreme Śiva.
Knowing the answers to the chapter's questions, the yogi first gains a yogic glory above all those rewards, then, becoming a knower, reaches Viṣṇu's supreme state, the root of the world.
Rituals, austerity, charity and study bring only temporary material rewards unless joined with devotion; yogis who grasp this attach their minds to God alone and reach eternal happiness.

verses.hook: What does the yogi gain beyond the rewards of rituals, study and charity?

refs.note: Good conduct, austerity, sacrifice, chanting and charity cannot cure the mind's worldly disease without devotion, so only devotion leads beyond temporary rewards.
